rv.q: The RSC production of Hilary Mantel's Thomas Cromwell novels is a theatrical triumph that transforms dense historical material into riveting drama.
The production achieves something close to miraculous: It makes you feel as if you were watching history unfold in real time.
The result is a pair of plays that are both intellectually stimulating and emotionally satisfying.
What makes this theatrical enterprise so compelling is the way it transforms what could be dusty historical pageantry into intimate, immediate drama.
These are productions of supreme intelligence and sensitivity, which honor both the complexity of Mantel's prose and the craft of theatrical storytelling.
The RSC's magnificent adaptation of Hilary Mantel's novels about Thomas Cromwell arrives on Broadway with most of its power intact, offering a masterclass in ensemble acting.
Still, as a fast-paced political thriller, it is fiendishly engaging, and director Jeremy Herrin’s 23-member corps skillfully slips in and out of multiple roles.
Of course, those fits of pique can land people in the Tower, a sobering reality that closes this absorbing, uncommonly ambitious chronicle on a chilling note.
The acting is led by an indefatigable Ben Miles, whose Cromwell is watchful, patient and sardonic.
It is hard not to wish for something deeper from all those hours onstage.
We get the brutalism of it all, but rather miss the emotion; even the obvious heart-wrenchers are gracefully elided.
As well-acted, grandly staged and beautifully lit as it is, the show still manages to be tedious
This is a magnificent evening in the theater that brings history to life with intelligence, wit and dramatic power that will leave you breathless.
The immensely talented actors manage to make every backroom deal, courtier spat, and royal tantrum fully enjoyable.
Wolf Hall brings out the best in Broadway, transforming what could have been a stuffy history lesson into riveting theater that makes the Tudor court feel immediate and alive.
The show is shot through with sly parries and juicy jabs.

Miles closely resembles Robert Stack in that vintage TV series “The Untouchables”: He maintains an implacable façade regardless of what he’s thinking, and that Miles rivets our attention for six hours makes his performance a masterclass in minimalist acting.
But is it the subtle, engrossing, mysterious masterpiece that Mantel's novels deserved?
The supple performances provided by these and other cast members cannot, however, compensate for plays that impress but don't transport us.
But is it the subtle, engrossing, mysterious masterpiece that Mantel's novels deserved?
Although full of intrigue and cruel twists of fate, “Wolf Hall” is a stiff, step-by-step, plodding march through English history, leaving little space for character development.
But what shocked me was how dull I found it.
